paraphrase: A perfected brāhmaṇa teaches Kāśyapa: how the jīva leaves the body at death and takes a new one according to its deeds, the formation of the embryo, and liberation through yoga — holding the mind within the body, one sees the self that is free.
Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna: that dharma was fully sufficient for reaching the state of Brahman; I cannot tell it again in full as I did then.
speaker: Kṛṣṇa

notes: Kṛṣṇa adds that he spoke it then yoked in yoga, and instead relates an ancient story (14.16).

paraphrase: The brāhmaṇa to his wife: smell, tongue, eye, skin, ear, mind and understanding are the seven tongues of the fire Vaiśvānara within; the smellable, drinkable, visible, touchable, audible, thinkable and knowable are the seven fuel-sticks; the smeller, eater, seer, toucher, hearer, thinker and knower are the seven great priests; offering these oblations duly into the seven fires, the wise produce (the worlds) in their own sources.
notes: Verse ref checked against the local digitized text (Critical Edition).

paraphrase: The royal sage Alarka resolves to shoot arrows at mind, nose, tongue, skin, ear and eye; each answers that his arrows will not pierce it but his own vitals; he then turns to yoga and by it conquers the senses.
notes: 14.30.2–16 (the refrain 'these arrows will not pass through me') checked.

paraphrase: Brahmā teaches the sages the three guṇas — tamas, rajas and sattva — their marks, their mutual dependence, and the destinies of those in whom each prevails.
The eternal tree of Brahman — with the great elements as its boughs and the particulars as its twigs, ever in leaf and flower, bearing fruits good and bad — is the livelihood of all beings.
notes: The chapter continues that cutting this tree with the sword of knowledge one attains immortality (not verse-checked).
